title: Clubroot: How to Spot It and Stop It in Cabbage and Pechay
metaTitle: Clubroot of Cabbage: Signs, Causes and Control
metaDescription: Clubroot swells cabbage roots into clubs and can stay in the soil for 10 years or more. Learn the signs, how lime helps, and how to keep it out.
excerpt: Clubroot is a soil disease of cabbage, Chinese cabbage, pechay and the other crucifers. It swells the roots into thick clubs, so the plant wilts, yellows and fails to head. Once it is in a field it stays for years, so this page shows how to spot it, slow it and keep it out.

heroImage.alt: A cabbage family plant pulled up to show its swollen, knotted clubroot galls

blocks.text:
Clubroot comes from Plasmodiophora brassicae, a soil organism that is not a true fungus. The Pacific Pests and Pathogens sheet places it in a separate group of protists. Every member of the cabbage family can catch it, including the weeds. Chinese cabbage, head cabbage, broccoli and turnip are very susceptible, while cauliflower suffers a little less.

In the Philippines, a 1983 survey in Philippine Phytopathology found clubroot serious in some cabbage fields of Atok, Benguet, and suspected it in Bangao and Buguias. The authors warned that it could limit cabbage production there. The acid soils and the intensive cropping favor it. Later, Benguet State University tested lime and friendly fungi against it. If your cabbage wilts in moist soil, pull a plant and check the roots.

blocks.caption: Quick facts
rows: Cabbage, Chinese cabbage, pechay, broccoli, cauliflower and other crucifers
Roots and base, the whole plant and seedlings
It infects from the seedbed onward in wet, acid soil at about 20 to 25 degrees Celsius. So cool, wet highland fields are at risk.
Resting spores live in the soil for 10 years or more. They move with soil water, runoff, muddy boots and tools, and on the roots of infected seedlings.

blocks.text: Pull up a wilting plant and wash the roots. Clubroot turns them into swollen, twisted, club shaped lumps with few fine roots. New infections show small galls of 1 to 20 mm, while old ones form long, spindle shaped clubs. Above ground, the leaves look pale green, yellow, purplish or blue green. They also wilt even in moist soil. Root knot nematodes also make galls. But theirs are small beads along the roots, while clubroot makes big clubs.

items: Plants wilt even when the soil is moist.
Leaves turn pale green, yellow or purplish, and the plants stay small.
Pulled roots show thick, swollen, club shaped lumps with few fine roots.
Heads fail to form or stay too small to sell when the plants are infected late.
Badly infected plants wilt for good, and their leaves rot.

blocks.title: Do not confuse it with
blocks.text: Root knot nematode galls are the usual mixup. Nematode galls are small and bead like along the roots, while clubroot makes large, spindle shaped clubs, mostly on the main roots of cabbage family crops.

Clubroot kills by thirst. The clubs block water uptake, so early infections stunt the plants, and later ones stop the heads from forming. The Pacific Pests and Pathogens sheet reports yearly losses of at least 10 percent in brassica crops in Australia, with total crop loss possible over time. Worse, once a field is infested, the resting spores stay alive for 10 years or more.

The disease needs four things: acid soil below pH 7, wet soil, about 20 to 25 degrees Celsius, and a host crop. That is why cool, wet highland fields suffer. In a Benguet State University trial, lime plus the friendly fungus Paecilomyces lilacinus gave about 70 percent control. Lime alone gave about 59 percent. So lime is the backbone of control, and no spray cures a clubbed root.

items: Raise the soil pH. NC State Extension advises liming to a pH of 7.1 to 7.5, and the Benguet trial found lime alone gave about 59 percent control. Have the soil tested first, and lime before transplanting.

Plant only clean seedlings. Raise them in clean trays with pasteurized or soilless mix. Never buy seedlings from a field with clubroot, since the 1983 Benguet survey traced spread to infected seedlings.
Drain the field. Use raised beds and open canals, because wet soil lets the spores swim to the roots.
Add biological help to the lime. In the Benguet State University trial, Paecilomyces lilacinus plus lime gave the best result, about 70 percent control.

Keep the spores home. Wash soil off boots, tools and tillers before you move from an infested field to a clean one. The [diamondback moth](/pests/diamondback-moth) also cut yields in that trial, so manage both.

blocks.text: The Pacific Pests and Pathogens sheet says no chemicals are available to smallholders for clubroot. In the United States, NC State lists fluazinam and cyazofamid as registered for it, applied to the soil before or at transplanting. Check the FPA registration in the Philippines before you use either, and follow the label.

blocks.caption: Active ingredients that work. Always follow the label of an FPA registered product.
rows: soil treatment at transplanting, registered for clubroot in some countries
soil treatment, registered for clubroot in the United States

blocks.title: Spray safely
blocks.text: Use only products registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label for the rate, the timing and the protective clothing. Switch to a different fungicide group next time, so the disease does not learn to survive it. Our [guide to plant diseases](/diseases/plant-diseases-philippines) explains how.

items: Rotate away from all crucifers for 4 to 7 years where the disease has been found.
Pull cabbage family weeds in and around the field, since they host the disease too.
Collect and burn the old roots and plant debris, and never compost infected plants.
Plow deeply and keep the field well drained, and test the soil pH before every cabbage crop. A field with clubbed roots may also have [black rot](/diseases/black-rot), so check the leaves too.

items.a: A soil organism called Plasmodiophora brassicae. It is not a true fungus. It infects the roots of cabbage family crops in wet, acid soil. Then it leaves resting spores that survive for 10 years or more.

Lime does not cure plants already sick, but it cuts new infections. NC State advises raising the soil pH to 7.1 to 7.5. In a Benguet State University trial, lime alone gave about 59 percent control, and lime plus Paecilomyces lilacinus gave about 70 percent.

items.q: How is clubroot different from root knot nematode?
items.a: Both swell the roots. [Root knot nematode](/diseases/root-knot-nematode) makes small, bead like galls on many crops, while clubroot makes large clubs only on cabbage family crops.
